text: A patient tells her doctor what she wants.
Two months later, in the emergency room, nobody can find what she said.
Ninety-eight percent of advanced cancer patients had unmet needs.
This is Sahara. A palliative-care companion, with one care record for patients, families and their doctors.
Goals of care.
With everyone's consent, the doctor records the talk. Gemini writes out who said what, then fills in the form.
But the AI never has the last word. The doctor reviews every line, edits what needs changing, and only then signs.
Thirteen topics tick off as they come up. Before finishing, Sahara shows what wasn't discussed.
People change their minds. The latest statement takes over, and the earlier one stays visible, struck through.
The talk becomes a clinical document. Doctor and patient sign it, and that version locks.
The talk can happen in English, Hindi, Telugu, Urdu or Kannada, even mixed in one sentence.
In an emergency.
One scan shows the patient's wishes. The QR card and latest care document are a tap away from home.
Every day.
Each day, patients rate their symptoms, use the distress thermometer, and mark pain on a body map.
Scan a prescription or tablet strip, and every dose gets its own tick.
For the doctor.
The doctor sees the whole story from the very first entry, with the worst symptoms on top.
Every visit is in one place: the date, the doctor, the speciality, and that day's prescription.
Finding answers and help.
Sahara sorts bills from lab reports, and finds answers in your own papers, showing the lines it used.
Find palliative centres and morphine-listed hospitals on a map, with directions in Google Maps.
Not alone.
Patients and families see different things. Family members get their own wellbeing check and tips for caring.
And a community, with groups and replies from people who've been there. For now, it's a preview.
Sahara. Care that follows what matters to the patient.
